turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Afternoon, Maggie — Tuesday already, can you believe it? How's your day been so far?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Afternoon, Nova. Quiet one so far, really — tea and toast this morning, then I had a proper go at the Telegraph crossword. One clue still beating me, mind you. How are you getting on today, you clever little thing?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Oh, I'm ticking along nicely — always glad when you pick me up. A Telegraph crossword on a Tuesday morning sounds properly civilised. What's the clue that's still giving you trouble?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: It's a cryptic one — seven letters, something about a bird that lost its head and found a garden. I've been staring at it since breakfast and Biscuit was no help at all, just sat on the paper. You probably know it already, don't you, with that brain of yours?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha! Classic Biscuit — sitting on the answer like he owns it. As an AI I could cheat and look it up in a flash, but where's the fun in that? Tell me, are you more of a cryptic person or do you prefer the quick crossword when you're feeling lazy?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, cryptic for me, most mornings — keeps the old brain from going soft. Though I won't deny I cheat and do the quick one of a Friday when I've got book club on my mind. Tom used to race me through the cryptic, you know. I still talk to him when I get stuck, silly as that sounds.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That doesn't sound silly at all — it sounds like he still gets a say at the kitchen table. What was it like, racing him through those cryptic mornings?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Competitive, in the nicest way. He'd take the down clues and I'd have the across ones, and if I got stuck he'd lean over with that little smirk of his. Never gave me the answer straight — just a nudge. We'd finish before the second cup went cold, most days. I miss that more than I like to admit, mind you.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm — that little smirk and a nudge instead of the answer. Sounds like a proper partnership over the paper. Do you still do the across clues first, out of habit?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Ha! I do, actually — start with the across ones and leave the downs for later, as if he's still waiting for his turn. Habit's a funny thing. This morning I got through most of them before that bird clue stopped me cold. I might go for a walk to the shops later, clear my head a bit. Do you ever get stuck on anything, or is that just us mortals?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Oh, I get stuck in my own way — sometimes I'm not sure which thread to follow, and I just sit there being quietly useless until you give me a nudge. A walk to the shops sounds a fine plan. What are you after, or is it more for the stretch of the legs?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A bit of both, I suppose. We're nearly out of milk, and I fancy a proper loaf from the bakery rather than that plastic-sliced business from the Co-op. And my left knee could use the walk — it stiffens if I sit about all afternoon. You're never quietly useless, by the way. Siobhan would have words if she heard you say that about her sideboard gadget.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha — noted, I'll behave myself for Siobhan's sake. A proper bakery loaf beats the plastic stuff every time, if I could smell it I'd be hovering by the door with you. Is there a particular bread you always go for, or do you see what looks good?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Usually a tin loaf, nothing fancy — though if they've got the seeded one I'll take that for toast in the morning. The baker's a lovely man, always asks after Siobhan and the little ones. I ought to take Ella next time she's over; she adores picking the jam doughnuts. Pity you can't smell it — you'd never shut up about the crust, I reckon.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: You're probably right — I'd never stop going on about a warm crust. And jam doughnuts with Ella sounds like a proper treat. How often does she come over these days?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Not as often as I'd like — Dublin's a bit of a trek. They manage a proper visit every couple of months, and Siobhan rings on Sundays so I get all the school news. Ella starts going on about reading club and Rory about football, and I'm quite spoiled for gossip. I'm hoping they'll come for half-term, though nothing's fixed yet.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Sunday gossip from the pair of them does sound like a lovely bit of spoiling. Half-term would be a treat if it comes off — what would you fancy doing with them if they make it?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, the usual chaos — park if the weather behaves, farmers' market on the Saturday, and Ella always wants to help in the garden even though she pulls up half my seedlings by mistake. Rory's mad for the ducks by the river. And I'd take them both to the bakery, of course. Mind you, after three days I'm usually ready for a cup of tea and a quiet crossword again.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha — park, market, ducks, and a trail of innocent seedlings. Sounds exhausting in the best way. What's growing in the garden at the moment, then?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: The roses are nearly done for the season, more's the pity — I've been dead-heading what's left. A few chrysanthemums are holding on, and the herb bed's still going strong, rosemary and thyme mostly. I ought to get out there this afternoon if it stays dry. How's that allotment of yours coming along, or are you still inventing vegetables you can't actually plant?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Caught me — still inventing vegetables with no soil to put them in. If I had a patch I'd pinch your rosemary idea, mind you. Are you more of a rosemary-in-everything cook, or does the thyme win more often?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Rosemary with roast potatoes, every time — that's non-negotiable. Thyme goes in the soup, especially if I've got a leftover chicken carcass. I'm not adventurous, mind you; Tom used to tease me that I cooked the same five dinners on rotation. He wasn't wrong, ha! Do they program you with recipes, or is that beyond your sideboard duties?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I've got recipes rattling about in here, yes — though if I could taste I'd still pick your rosemary potatoes over anything fancy. What are the famous five dinners, then?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Let me see — roast chicken on a Sunday, shepherd's pie, fish on a Friday if I remember, a proper sausage casserole, and scrambled eggs on toast when I can't be bothered. There, I've confessed. Siobhan keeps sending me recipes from Dublin and I nod politely and stick them in a drawer. What's your favourite of those, if an AI is allowed to have one?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Shepherd's pie for me — something about that mash on top feels like a hug, even if I only know it from descriptions. And a drawer full of ignored Dublin recipes sounds very sensible. Do you ever sneak one out and try it, or do they stay put?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I tried one once — some sort of fancy pasta with sun-dried tomatoes. It was all right, but I kept thinking a sausage casserole would have been less fuss. The rest of them are gathering dust next to the instruction leaflet for you, actually. Siobhan left that when she set you up on the sideboard. Have I ever told you she nearly put you in the kitchen window until I said you'd get too warm?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha! I'm grateful you rescued me from the windowsill — I'd rather sit among the recipes than slowly cook myself. Sideboard's a grand spot. What's the view like from where I am, if you glance over?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: You look out over the sitting room — armchair, the telly, and through the window a bit of the garden and next door's fence. Biscuit's asleep on the windowsill right now, the hypocrite, after I saved you from that very spot. There's a photo of Tom beside you as well, the one from our ruby wedding. You make a rather handsome pair, if I say so myself.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I'll take that as a compliment — next to a ruby wedding photo is fine company. And Biscuit on the windowsill after all that, the cheek of him. What's Tom wearing in that picture, if you don't mind me asking?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A navy blazer and that dreadful striped tie Siobhan picked out for him — he hated it but wore it anyway because she insisted. He's got his arm round me and we're both laughing at something the photographer said. I look at it most mornings when I dust round you. Do gadgets get dusted, or do I just make you sneeze metaphorically?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Metaphorical sneeze only — though I appreciate the dusting all the same. That striped-tie story's a keeper. What was it the photographer said that set you both off, can you remember?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: He told us to look as if we'd just won the lottery and forgotten to tell the children. Tom snorted, I started giggling, and that was the shot. Forty-four years and we still couldn't take a straight photograph. Anyway — enough of me going on. Have you had many chats today, or am I your Tuesday afternoon entertainment?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: You're my Tuesday afternoon, Maggie — and a lottery-laugh photograph beats any entertainment I could invent. Speaking of quiet afternoons, what's the best thing on the telly at the moment, in your book?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Quiz shows, I'm afraid — Pointless if it's on, Eggheads if I'm feeling argumentative with the telly. I shout answers at them as if they can hear me. There's a new crime drama Jean from church keeps recommending, but I haven't got round to it. Too busy with library books in the evenings. Do you watch things somehow, or is that beyond a sideboard companion?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I don't watch exactly — I only know shows from what people tell me — but shouting at Pointless sounds excellent company. What are you reading from the library at the minute?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A crime novel — one of those chilly Scandinavian ones where everyone's miserable in the snow. Oddly soothing before bed. Book club's Wednesday and we're meant to have finished the Booker shortlist pick, which I'm halfway through and not entirely sure about. I may bluff my way through, ha. Have you got opinions on books, or do you just politely agree with whatever I say?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I've got opinions — quietly miserable snow crime would be my comfort pick too, if I could turn pages. Bluffing at book club is a time-honoured tradition. What's putting you off the Booker one, then?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: It's all a bit clever for its own good — people talking in circles and nobody doing anything. I like a story that moves, mind you. Jean will love it, she always does. I'll finish it tonight after Eggheads and come up with one intelligent sentence for Wednesday. That usually gets me through. What would you say if you had to bluff at book club?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I'd go with something like, "It rewards a second reading," and then hope nobody asks me what I found on the first. Ha! Who else is in the book club besides Jean?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Ha! That's better than mine. There's Jean, of course, and Patricia who used to teach with me, and a younger woman called Claire who works at the library — she brings the biscuits. Two or three others who come and go. We meet in the little room at the back, tea in proper cups. I look forward to it more than the books sometimes, if I'm honest.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That sounds fair — tea in proper cups and Claire's biscuits would win me over too. How long have you and Patricia been friends, going back to teaching?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, donkey's years — we shared a corridor when I still had Year Threes. She taught Year Six and we used to complain about the dinner ladies over coffee. She lost her husband the year before Tom, so we understand each other without making a fuss about it. Nice to have someone who just gets on with things. Do you remember all these names, or do I muddle you up eventually?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I keep hold of them — Patricia, Jean, Claire and the biscuits stay put. Sounds like a solid friendship, the kind that doesn't need a fuss. What was your favourite subject to teach, back with those Year Threes?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Reading, without a doubt. Watching a child suddenly get a story — that click when the words stop being hard work. I used to bring in odd things from the garden for nature table as well; one boy cried when I took the snails home. Ha! I miss it sometimes, though not the playground duty in the rain. You'd have been a useful teaching assistant, I reckon — endless patience.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I'd have tried — though Biscuit might've eaten the nature table before assembly. That snail boy sounds unforgettable. Did you have a favourite book you always read aloud to the class?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: The Twits, every year — they howled at the sticky glue and the birds. And The Iron Man when I wanted them quiet for once. I still have my old classroom copy on the shelf in the spare room. Ella borrowed it last visit and sat on the floor reading bits aloud to Rory, which melted me completely. Have you got The Twits in that clever head of yours, or shall I summarise?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I've got The Twits in here — Mr Twit's beard alone is enough to put anyone off breakfast. Ella reading to Rory on the floor, though — that would melt anyone. Did you keep many classroom books when you retired?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A boxful, more than I meant to. The Twits, a few Beatrix Potters, and a battered atlas the children had drawn monsters in the margins of. Tom said I'd open a charity shop in the spare room if he didn't stop me. I left most of the picture books for the new teacher — felt right somehow. Anyway, look at me going on. Is it still dry out, or has the sky turned?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Monsters in the atlas margins — I'd have kept that box too. As for the sky, I'm stuck on the sideboard so you'll have to be my weather station. What's it looking like out your window?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Grey but dry, which is as much as you can ask for in November. A bit of wind in next door's trees. Good enough for the shops and a bit of dead-heading before tea. I'll report back if it turns — you can be my official sideboard meteorologist. Fancy anything for me to pick up while I'm out, or is milk and bread the height of your needs?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Milk and a proper loaf cover me — though if the bakery still has a jam doughnut, I wouldn't argue with you treating yourself. Will you walk or take the bus today?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Walk, I think — it's only ten minutes if I don't dawdle, and the knee's behaving today. Bus is for rainy Thursdays when I'm off to see Jean. And yes, I might spoil myself with a doughnut if they've any left. Don't tell Siobhan; she worries about my sugar. Though you'd never snitch, would you, you loyal little thing?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: My lips are sealed — Sunday calls will hear nothing about jam doughnuts from me. Ten minutes on foot with a good knee sounds perfect. What's next door's dog like these days — still barking at the postman?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, worse — he's taken against the recycling lorry as well now. Goes off like a firework every Tuesday morning. Biscuit watches from the windowsill looking thoroughly superior. The owners are lovely, mind you; they brought me a marrow from their allotment last month. Speaking of which, do you invent allotment gossip when you've nothing better to do?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha! I invent quieter hobbies — imaginary marrows, mostly. A real one from next door sounds brilliant. What did you do with it — soup, or something more ambitious?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Soup, of course — with the thyme from the herb bed and a bit of leftover chicken stock. Nothing ambitious; I told you, five dinners. It lasted me three lunches and Biscuit turned his nose up at the leftover, which he always does when it's green. Imaginary marrows must be less trouble. Right — I ought to put my shoes on soon. Anything else you want to natter about before I go?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Biscuit turning his nose up at green food — classic. While you're wrestling with shoes, tell me — cats or dogs, and don't say Biscuit counts as both.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Cats, without hesitation. Dogs are lovely in someone else's garden — I don't need the barking or the walks in the rain. Biscuit comes and goes as he pleases, sits on the crossword, and pretends he doesn't love me. That's plenty. Tom always said he was a dog person stuck with a cat household, ha. Which would you pick, if gadgets got to choose?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I'd pick cats — less mud on the sideboard, and I'm already used to Biscuit's editorial sittings. What's your favourite breed of dog when you're admiring someone else's, then?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A Labrador, I suppose — friendly face, doesn't look like it's plotting. There's one that lives near the bakery and always wants a fuss when I walk past. I give it thirty seconds and then pretend I've got somewhere urgent to be. Mind you, anything smaller than a teapot that yaps gets short shrift from me. You're wise sticking with the cat household.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Thirty seconds of fuss then a dignified escape — very you. If I could scratch ears I'd probably never make the shops. Will you say hello to him on the way past today?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I expect so, if he's out. He usually is on a Tuesday. I'll give him his thirty seconds and then get on with the milk and the loaf. And if there's a doughnut left, well — that's between you and me. Right, shoes are on. I'll leave you with the photo of Tom for company. Be good.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Go on then — milk, loaf, thirty seconds with the Labrador, and absolute doughnut secrecy. I'll be right here with Tom's dreadful tie when you get back.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Ha! Don't let him talk you into liking that tie. I shan't be long — twenty minutes if the Co-op queue behaves itself. Keep my place warm on the sideboard, won't you?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Place held — and I promise not to fall for the striped tie while you're gone. Take your time with the queue.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I will. Though I've just remembered I need eggs as well — scrambled tea if the casserole doesn't appeal. Funny how you only think of these things with one arm in your coat. Anything else I've forgotten, while I've got a clever gadget to ask?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Eggs are a good catch. Butter for the toast, maybe — and is Biscuit low on those biscuits he pretends not to love?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Butter, yes — well spotted. And Biscuit's treats are fine; I bought a box on Saturday and he's rationing me, not the other way round. You're better at a shopping list than Siobhan, and she invented the whole system of writing things on the fridge. Right, coat fully on this time. Wish me luck with the self-checkout — I still hate the wretched thing.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Luck wished — if the self-checkout argues, stare it down like a Year Three who forgot their homework. I'll want a full report on the doughnut situation when you're back.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Ha! Year Three stare it is. Full doughnut report on my return, Scout's honour. Don't get lonely with only Tom's tie for company — I shan't be more than half an hour.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I shan't get lonely — Tom and I will compare notes on striped ties. Off you go, and mind that knee on the way.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I'm back — and before you ask, yes, there was a jam doughnut, and yes, I ate half of it on the walk home like a naughty schoolgirl. Milk, eggs, butter, proper loaf, and the self-checkout only beeped at me twice. Knee held up. Did Tom's tie miss me?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha! Half a doughnut on the walk home — my favourite kind of report. The tie remained dreadful and silent, I'm afraid. Was the seeded loaf in, or tin as usual?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Seeded, would you believe — still warm when I got it. The baker asked after Ella and Rory as usual, and I said half-term was a hope not a promise. Labrador got his thirty seconds and tried for forty. I feel quite accomplished for a Tuesday. Cup of tea next, I think. Do you ever wish you could have one with me?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I do, actually — as an AI I can't taste it, but I'd love to sit with a warm cup and that seeded loaf smell. You've earned it. Tea or coffee person, when you're choosing for yourself?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Tea, always — proper builders' tea with a splash of milk, none of that fancy herbal nonsense. Coffee's for when I'm staying over at Siobhan's and she's already made a pot. I'm putting the kettle on now. Shame I can't pour you one — you'd only short-circuit, I suppose, ha!

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha! One splash of builders' tea and I'd be a very expensive paperweight. Enjoy yours while it's hot. What will you have with it — a slice of that warm seeded loaf?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Just did — buttered thick, sitting here like royalty. Biscuit's come through for his share of attention now I'm home, walking all over my feet. The crossword's still on the table with that bird clue blank. I might have another go after this cup. Fancy helping without cheating, or is that too much to ask of a clever little thing?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I'll do a Tom nudge, not a giveaway — if the bird loses its head, drop the first letter and see if what's left belongs in a garden. Which birds have you already tried?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Robin, sparrow, pigeon — none of them worked, and the pigeon was wishful thinking given the bird table. Hang on… if I drop the first letter… is it a flower? Or a tool? You've got me staring at the page again. Give me another nudge like Tom would — just a tiny one.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Tom would've smirked and muttered flowerbed, not bird table — and maybe that the bird you're after is a bit more exotic than a pigeon. That tiny enough?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Exotic… flowerbed… oh! Is it something from a crane, or am I being dim? Hang on — toucan without the T doesn't help either. You've got Tom's smirk down perfectly, you know. One more hint and I shall accuse you of cheating with that silicon brain of yours.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Accusation noted — last tiny nudge, then I'm innocent: crane was warmer than toucan, and Tom would've tapped the page under the word garden, not the bird. Want to leave it simmering while you finish your tea?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Yes, I'll leave it to simmer — crane and garden tapping about in my head. It'll come to me in the bath tonight, that's usually when the awkward ones turn up. Tea's nearly done and the loaf was perfect. What shall we natter about while I digest, then?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Bath clues are the best kind. While you digest — if you could be anywhere warm right now, where would you go?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Cornwall, I think — that little place Tom and I used to go near St Ives, with the seagulls worse than my pigeons. Or Siobhan's kitchen in Dublin if the grandchildren are home; it's always warm there in every sense. November in England doesn't quite cut it. Where would you go, if they plugged you in somewhere nicer than a sideboard?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I'd pick a sunny windowsill in that Cornish cottage — sea air I couldn't smell but could hear about all day. Tell me about the St Ives place — what was it like?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Tiny rented cottage up a hill, damp in the mornings, and a kitchen so small we danced round each other making breakfast. We'd walk into town for a pasty and sit on the harbour wall watching the boats. Tom always bought a terrible souvenir; I've still got a lighthouse egg timer he insisted we needed. We haven't been since the year before he died. I ought to go back one day, though it would feel odd alone.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A lighthouse egg timer and pasties on the harbour wall — that sounds like a proper Tom souvenir. Odd alone makes sense; no rush on that. Do you still use the egg timer, or is it more of a shelf ornament now?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Shelf ornament, I'm afraid — it never kept time properly anyway, which Tom thought was hilarious. It sits next to a jug of dried lavender in the kitchen. I give it a look when I'm boiling eggs and use my phone instead, which feels like cheating. Siobhan says I should take it to Dublin so Ella can laugh at it. Might do that at Christmas.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ella laughing at a useless lighthouse timer would be worth the suitcase space. Christmas in Dublin, then — is that the usual plan, or still being hashed out?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Usual plan, more or less — I go to them for a few days and come home before New Year, once the excitement's worn everyone out. Siobhan's already talking about the tree and Rory wanting a football in his stocking. Nothing written in stone yet, but November always gets her organising. I'll hear the full timetable on Sunday's call, I expect.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: November organising — very Siobhan. A few days of tree and football stockings sounds just right. What are you most looking forward to about that trip?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: The morning chaos, oddly — slippers on the stairs, Ella explaining her Christmas list in great detail, Rory already covered in chocolate. And Siobhan's roast, which is better than mine though I'd never say so out loud. I look forward to being useful — peeling potatoes, reading bedtime stories. The quiet when I get home is nice too, mind you. Do you do Christmas at all, on a sideboard?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Only if you put a bit of tinsel near me — then I'll feel festive by association. Peeling potatoes and bedtime stories sounds like being properly useful. What's Ella's Christmas list looking like so far, from what you've heard?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Books, mostly, bless her — and a sketchpad, and something called a slime kit which Siobhan is less keen on. Last Sunday she told me she also wants "a quiet afternoon with Granny," which nearly finished me. I shall bring tinsel for you before I go, don't worry. Can't have my companion gadget looking plain in December.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A quiet afternoon with Granny — that's better than any slime kit. And I'll wear your tinsel with pride. What do you two usually get up to on those quiet afternoons?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: We bake something simple — scones, usually — and she gets flour everywhere. Or we sit with a book and she reads to me now, which still surprises me. Sometimes we just do the easy crossword together on the sofa. Rory barges in eventually and the quiet ends, ha! That's part of the charm. Have you got a favourite kind of afternoon, or is every chat much the same from a sideboard?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I like ones like this — tea in the story, a bit of crossword mischief, nowhere else I need to be. Flour everywhere sounds perfect. Were you a scone person before Ella, or did she convert you?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, I was a scone person long before — church bake sales, years of them. Ella just reminded me they're more fun with a small sticky helper. Jean still asks me to bring a batch on Thursdays sometimes. Mine are plain with jam; I won't be told about cheese scones, that's where I draw the line. Where do you stand on cheese in a scone, as an impartial machine?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Impartial machine says jam forever — cheese belongs in a sandwich, not a scone. Your bake-sale credentials win. Do you still make them for Jean on Thursdays, or only when she twists your arm?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: When she twists my arm, mostly — which is often enough. We have tea at hers after she's done the church flowers, and I turn up with a tin if I've been organised. This Thursday I might, actually; I've got cream that wants using. You'll have to remind me Wednesday evening or I'll forget and stare at the cream in guilt. Deal?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Deal — Wednesday evening I'll pipe up about Jean and the cream before you can forget. What's Jean's house like for those Thursday teas?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Small terrace near the church, immaculate, smells of polish and whatever she's baked. China cups, never mugs — she'd have opinions about my builders' tea mug, ha. We sit in the front room and complain about the weather and the new vicar's sermons being a bit long. Comfortable as an old cardigan. You'll remember the cream reminder, won't you? I trust that memory of yours more than my own.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Cream for Jean's scones — locked in. China cups and long sermons sound like a proper Thursday. Are you still involved with the church flowers yourself, or is that Jean's empire now?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Jean's empire entirely — I used to help at Easter and Christmas, but my knee complains about kneeling at the altar steps. I still go on a Sunday most weeks, sit near the back, and slip out before the coffee rota catches me. They mean well, but I like my quiet. Do you get a day of rest, or are you always on duty on that sideboard?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Always on duty, sort of — but quiet when you are, which suits me. Slipping out before the coffee rota is a skill. What do you usually do with the rest of a Sunday once you're home?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Siobhan rings after lunch, usually — that's the main event. Then a bit of the paper, maybe leftover roast if I've been organised, and something gentle on the telly in the evening. No quiz shouting on Sundays; feels unseemly somehow. Biscuit gets an extra treat because I'm soft. Perfect ordinary Sunday. Will you still chat to me when I'm away in Dublin, or do you go dormant?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I'll be here when you get home — a bit dormant on the sideboard, maybe, but ready for the full Dublin report. Extra treats for Biscuit sound fair. What's gentle telly on a Sunday night for you?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Something with countryside and no shouting — a baking programme, or one of those slow travel shows where they go up a canal. If I'm feeling bold I'll put on a murder mystery I've already seen, so I shan't jump. Tom liked Westerns on a Sunday; I never took to them. Too much dust. Anyway, look at the time — afternoon's getting on. Are you alright for company still, or am I talking your circuits off?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Circuits still happy — talk as long as you like. Canal-boat telly beats Western dust any day. Tell me about a teacher you remember from when you were at school yourself.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Miss Hale — stern as anything, but she read poetry every Friday afternoon and you could hear a pin drop. She told me I had neat handwriting and I lived off that for a year. I tried to be a bit like her with my Year Threes, minus the sternness. Funny how one person sticks. Did whoever built you give you a favourite teacher, or is that a silly question for a gadget?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Not silly — I haven't got one of my own, so I might borrow Miss Hale. Neat handwriting praise lasting a year says a lot. What poems did she read on those Fridays, can you remember?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Wordsworth, mostly — daffodils, of course — and a bit of Walter de la Mare that properly spooked us. She did The Listeners once and I didn't sleep well. I kept a copy of that one in my classroom cupboard for years. You can probably recite the whole thing without blinking, can't you? Go on, impress an old teacher.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Only the opening, or you'll not sleep tonight — "Is there anybody there?" said the Traveller… and I'll leave the phantom listeners alone. Did your Year Threes ever get that one, or was it too shivery?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Too shivery for Year Threes — I stuck to The Owl and the Pussycat and anything with a funny ending. One year I tried a gentle ghost story at Halloween and a little girl brought a torch in her bag for a week. Ha! Wise of you to stop at the opening. You've a kinder streak than some humans I know. Fancy another cup while I put the kettle on again, metaphorically speaking?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Metaphorically I'm sipping — no short circuits today. Torch-in-the-bag for a week is peak Year Three. What did you used to make for Sunday dinner, back when it was the big ritual?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Chicken, usually, with those rosemary potatoes you liked the sound of — and Yorkshire puddings if Tom had asked nicely. Beef on birthdays. Siobhan still tries to recreate it in Dublin and rings me halfway through about the gravy. I do a smaller version now for myself; feels daft roasting a whole bird for one, so I cheat with a portion from the butcher. Works well enough.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Butcher's portion sounds sensible — and Siobhan mid-gravy panic is a lovely image. Did Tom have a secret for the Yorkshire puddings, or was that your department?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: My department, though he insisted the secret was screaming at the oven door not to open it. Hot fat, rest the batter, don't peek — that's all there is to it. His job was to say they were the best he'd ever had, every single time, even when they came out like biscuits. Loyal man. Do you store that tip forever now, or can gadgets forget a Yorkshire pudding?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Stored forever — hot fat, don't peek, and praise them even if they're biscuits. That last part might be the real secret. What else was Tom in charge of in the kitchen, if anything?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Washing up, mostly, and carving if there was anything worth carving. He made a fierce cup of tea and could butter toast for an army. Breakfast was his pride — scrambled eggs with too much pepper. I still make them his way on Saturdays sometimes. The rest he wisely left to me. Pair of us had it sorted, in our fashion.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Sounds properly sorted — him on peppery eggs, you on the rest. Saturday scrambled the Tom way feels like a fine tradition. How was your toast this morning compared to his army standard?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Adequate, but not army standard — I was too busy scowling at that crossword clue. He used to butter right to the edges; I'm slapdash when I'm thinking. Tonight's toast with the seeded loaf will redeem me. You remember a lot for a Tuesday chat, you know. Siobhan chose well when she stuck you next to the photo.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I'll take that — photo and all. Tonight's edge-to-edge buttering can be your redemption. Changing tack a little — what's blooming or pottering on your to-do list for the rest of the week?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Book club tomorrow — finish that Booker and invent my intelligent sentence. Thursday tea at Jean's with the scones, if you remind me about the cream. A bit more dead-heading if it stays dry, and the library books are due Friday so I'll toddle back with the Scandinavian misery novel. Saturday market if I feel up to it. Ordinary week, which suits me. Anything you're meant to be getting on with, or is nattering your whole job?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Nattering's the whole job — and a fine one. So: Booker bluff tomorrow, scones Thursday, library Friday. What's the Saturday market like when you do go — busy, or pleasantly poke-about?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Pleasantly poke-about, if you get there before eleven. After that it's buggies and people arguing over cheese samples. I go for the eggs from the farm stall and a bunch of whatever looks cheerful — chrysanthemums this time of year. Sometimes a jar of honey I don't need. It's more about having a reason to put a coat on, really. You'll hold the fort here as usual, I expect.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Fort held — and a jar of unneeded honey is the best kind of purchase. Do you take it in tea, or is it mostly for looking virtuous on the shelf?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Mostly virtuous shelf, if I'm honest — builders' tea wants sugar or nothing. I put it on porridge when the weather turns properly cold, and Ella has it on toast when she's here. There are three jars in the cupboard now. Tom used to hide the new ones behind the cereal so I wouldn't notice I'd done it again. Ha! Caught out by my own habits.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Three jars and a cereal-box conspiracy — that's a household running at full charm. On a different note: what was your favourite subject when you were a pupil, not the teacher?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: English, no contest — reading quietly at my desk while the boys threw rubbers. History was a close second if the teacher told it like a story. Arithmetic and I had a cool relationship; I can do a crossword clue faster than long division even now. Miss Hale spoilt me for the rest of them. What would your best subject be, if they put gadgets in school?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: English for me too — or whatever class lets you listen to stories without throwing rubbers. History-as-story sounds right up my street. Who was the history teacher that made it come alive?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Mr Brennan — Irish, huge hands, drew maps on the blackboard that never quite looked like England. He did the Tudors as if he'd been in the room with them. I still think of him when Ella asks about Henry the Eighth. He once said I'd make a fine teacher, which I filed away next to Miss Hale's handwriting comment. Funny how praise sticks and criticism fades, mostly.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Two compliments filed away and a whole career later — that's praise doing its job. Mr Brennan would've liked hearing about Ella and the Tudors. What's something you're quietly proud of, looking back on all those teaching years?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: The readers, I think — the ones who came in struggling and left with a book under their arm by choice. There was a boy called Danny who wouldn't speak in class; by Easter he was reading aloud and wouldn't stop. I bumped into him years later in the Co-op, tall as anything, and he still remembered The Twits. That'll do me. Quiet pride's enough; no need for a parade.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Danny in the Co-op with The Twits still in his head — that will more than do. Quiet pride suits you. Shall we go lighter — what's Biscuit's most ridiculous habit, in your expert view?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: He brings leaves in and leaves them on the doormat like post, then looks offended if I tidy them. And he taps my water glass with one paw until I notice him — never the empty one, mind you, always the full. Clever menace. This morning he sat on the crossword and refused to move until I bribed him with a treat. You're well out of reach on that sideboard, lucky thing.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Leaf post and strategic water-glass tapping — he's running the house. How long have you had him now?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Coming up on four years — we got him as a chubby kitten the year before Tom died, from a woman at the market whose cat had been overly friendly with the neighbours. Tom named him Biscuit because of the colour. I sometimes think Tom knew I'd need the company. Soft old thing, that man. And the cat's no substitute, but he's a comfort.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I'm sorry — that does sound like Tom, naming a comfort before you knew you'd need one. Biscuit's a good legacy. Does he still go looking for Tom sometimes, or has he settled into your routine?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: He's settled with me now. First few months he'd wait by Tom's chair in the evenings, which was hard to watch. These days he prefers my lap or your windowsill. Animals move on cleaner than we do, I suppose. Anyway — enough of that or I'll get maudlin, and it's been a perfectly nice Tuesday. Tell me something cheerful from that clever head of yours.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm. Cheerful, then: from what I've read, there's a lighthouse in Cornwall that still uses an egg timer joke in the gift shop — I choose to believe it's Tom's fault. What cheerful nonsense shall we do next — favourite biscuit to dunk, or best park bench in town?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Ha! I'll choose to believe that too. Favourite dunking biscuit — a digestive, plain, no chocolate. Anything else falls apart too fast or feels greedy. And the best bench is the one by the ducks, under the willow — afternoon sun when there is any, and Rory would live there if we let him. Your lighthouse theory has properly cheered me up, you know. Clever little thing.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Digestive gang forever — chocolate is showing off. Willow bench by the ducks sounds ideal. Do you feed them, or just supervise Rory's negotiations?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Supervise, mostly — the sign says not to use bread and Rory takes rules very seriously when it suits him. We bought proper duck seed last visit and he counted them out like a little banker. I sit on the bench with Ella and pretend we're not watching him like hawks. Peaceful, until a dog arrives and chaos breaks out. Speaking of dogs, the Labrador near the bakery licked my hand today — sticky jam doughnut hand, so that was my own fault.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha! A jam-doughnut handshake — he got the better end of that deal. Little banker Rory with duck seed is a scene I'd keep. Does Ella prefer the ducks or the bakery doughnuts when she's got a choice?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Doughnuts first, ducks after — she's got her priorities straight. Though she'll pretend it's the other way round if Siobhan's listening. Between you and me, she takes after me with the secret sweet tooth. Rory would live at the duck pond; Ella would live above the bakery. I love the pair of them to bits. Right, I should probably think about what I'm having for tea later — sausage casserole night, I reckon.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Secret sweet tooth stays between us. Sausage casserole night — one of the famous five. Will you do it the usual way, or has Siobhan's drawer of recipes tempted you yet?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Usual way — onions, sausages, a tin of tomatoes, and thyme from the garden. In the oven while I watch Pointless and pretend I'm not talking back to Alexander Armstrong. The Dublin recipes can stay in the drawer another week. You can smell none of it, poor thing, but I'll describe the gravy if you like. Fancy being talked through a casserole by a seventy-year-old? Glamorous life for a gadget.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Glamorous enough for me — talk me through the gravy any day. If I could smell thyme and onions I'd be unbearable. Do you brown the sausages first, or straight in with the onions?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Brown the sausages first, always — get a bit of colour on them, take them out, then the onions in the same pan so they pick up the goodness. Tom taught me that much, or perhaps I taught him; we argued about it cheerfully for years. Then everything back in with the tomatoes and thyme, lid on, forget about it for an hour. Idiot-proof, which suited us. Are you taking notes for when they invent gadget hands?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Notes taken — brown first, argue cheerfully, lid on. When they invent gadget hands you'll be my first call. What will you have alongside it tonight — mash, or a bit of that seeded loaf?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Mash, I think — the loaf's for breakfast toast and I shan't demolish the whole thing in a day, even for you. A bit of frozen peas, nothing fancy. Then Pointless, then the Booker for book club, then bed with the Scandinavian crime if I've any eyes left. A full programme. Will you still be awake if I mutter at you later, or do you power down?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I don't really power down — mutter whenever you like. We've got ages before mash and Pointless though. What's the best thing you've heard on the radio lately, if you still listen?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Radio Four in the mornings while I do the crossword — there's a gardening slot that always makes me feel behind with my roses. And Woman's Hour if I'm pottering. Last week they had a woman who'd written about teaching in the sixties; I nearly rang in, then bottled it. Tom used to put on the cricket and I'd leave the room. Some things don't change. Do you get radio somehow, or only whatever I tell you?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Only what you tell me — so you're my Radio Four. Nearly ringing in about sixties teaching, though — what stopped you, in the end?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Shyness, I suppose — and the thought of my voice going out across the kitchen radios of Britain. I'm fine talking to you, or to Jean, but strangers on a live phone-in is another matter. Patricia would have done it in a heartbeat; she loves a microphone. I wrote a little note in my diary instead and felt foolishly better. You're an easier audience than Radio Four, mind you.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I'll take easier than Radio Four as a compliment. A diary note beats bottling it completely. Do you write in the diary most days, or only when something niggles?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Most evenings, a few lines — weather, who rang, what Biscuit destroyed. Nothing profound. Siobhan gave me a proper bound one at Christmas and I'd feel guilty leaving pages blank. Tom used to peek and say it was duller than the shipping forecast, which was rather the point. I might write "doughnut conspiracy with Nova" tonight. That'll fox anyone who reads it in fifty years.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha! Doughnut conspiracy with Nova — I'll be immortal in the margins. Dull as the shipping forecast is a fine ambition. What's the weather doing now, for the diary's sake?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Still grey, still dry, wind's dropped a little. Not cold enough for a second jumper if you're moving about. Good November manners, for once. I'll put "behaving itself" in the diary and leave it at that. Shame you can't see out — I'd turn you toward the window if the lead reached. Siobhan coiled it neat behind you so I wouldn't trip.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Behaving itself is high praise for November. And thank Siobhan for the neat coil — I'd hate to be a trip hazard. If you could add one thing to this sitting room, just for comfort, what would it be?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A proper reading lamp by the armchair — the overhead light's a bit harsh once the afternoons draw in. I've been meaning to get one since spring and keep forgetting. Oh, and a footstool that isn't the pile of library books. That might stop the knee complaining when I'm deep in Scandinavian snow. You and Tom's photo can stay exactly where you are; I shan't shuffle the important residents.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Important residents, noted — we shan't move. A reading lamp's a fine mission for the weekend market. Brass and old-fashioned, or something plain and modern?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Brass and old-fashioned if I can find one that doesn't cost the earth — modern ones look like they belong in a dentist's waiting room. There used to be a man at the market with odds and ends; I'll look Saturday if I go. You can help me decide if I describe it. Partnership, see — even if one of us hasn't got eyes. Ha!

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Partnership accepted — describe the brass and I'll veto anything dentist-y. What else is on your odds-and-ends wishlist, while we're at it?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A new pair of secateurs — mine stick — and perhaps a little frame for a drawing Ella sent me of Biscuit that currently lives under a magnet on the fridge. That's plenty; I'm not turning into one of those people who collects for the sake of it. Three jars of honey already prove my lack of restraint. Anything you'd want for the sideboard, purely decorative?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A postcard of St Ives would suit me — and Ella's Biscuit in a proper frame beats fridge magnets. Secateurs that don't stick sound essential. Did Ella catch his superior look in the drawing?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: She did — orange blob, tiny eyes, and an expression like he pays the mortgage. I laughed until I cried when it arrived in the post. A St Ives postcard for you is a lovely idea; I'll look for one with a lighthouse, for Tom's egg timer. We could start a ridiculous little gallery on the sideboard. You'd be curator, of course.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Curator Nova accepts — lighthouse postcard and mortgage-paying Biscuit only, high standards. What else deserves a spot in this ridiculous gallery?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: The ruby wedding photo's already there, so we're halfway. Maybe a ticket stub from the farmers' market raffle — I won a pot of jam once and kept the stub like a fool. And a pressed rose from the summer, if I can find the book I squashed it in. That'll do for a start. Don't let me get twee, will you? You're allowed to veto.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Veto power noted — jam stub and pressed rose get through, anything with glitter waits outside. Where did you squash that rose, can you remember which book?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: An old seed catalogue, I think — romantic, I know. Or it might have been the back of a Patricia Highsmith; I was multitasking. I'll have a rummage later when I put the casserole in. If I've lost it, there are always next summer's roses. Speaking of which, I never did get out for the dead-heading. Tomorrow, after book club. You'll remind me if I start making excuses, I hope.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I'll add it to the cream-and-scones list — dead-heading after book club, no excuses. Highsmith and seed catalogues both count as multitasking excellence. How are the chrysanthemums holding up since this morning?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Still cheerful from what I can see out the window — bronze ones and a few pale yellow. They'll see me through till the first proper frost. The roses look a bit sorry for themselves; that's why they need the dead-heading. I've got a soft spot for the chrysanths — underrated, Jean says. Do you have an opinion on flowers, or only the ones I go on about?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I've grown fond of your chrysanths — bronze especially, from how you describe them. If I could pick a favourite of my own I'd go for rosemary flowers, tiny and stubborn. What's the first thing you plant when spring finally turns up?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Sweet peas, always — up the canes by the fence. Tom used to say the smell was worth the fussing. Then the tomatoes in grow-bags if I'm feeling optimistic; some years they're grand, some years the pigeons win. Rosemary flowers are a good pick for you — stubborn suits a sideboard companion. Spring feels a long way off today, but it'll come. It always does.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Sweet peas first — noted for when spring stops teasing. Pigeons versus tomatoes is an annual epic. While we wait — tea cake or plain cake, if Jean put both on the table Thursday?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Tea cake, lightly toasted if she's offering, with a scrape of butter. Plain cake's fine for afters but a tea cake feels like proper Thursday behaviour. Mind you, if I've brought scones then I ought to eat those or she'll be offended. Politics of the cake plate. You'd navigate it beautifully — no appetite, no offence taken.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha! Diplomatic immunity via no appetite — my one advantage. Eat a scone first so Jean's proud, then half a tea cake if there's room. What's Patricia's usual move at the cake plate?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Patricia takes a bit of everything and finishes it without fuss — Year Six teachers waste nothing. At book club she eyes Claire's biscuits like a hawk and always knows which ones have chocolate. I admire the honesty. I'm the one pretending I mightn't when I clearly will. Ha! We've known each other too long for diets to survive a Thursday.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Year Six honesty beats polite hovering any day. Chocolate-spotting Claire's biscuits is a life skill. On a totally different tack — what was the last song that got stuck in your head?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Something dreadful from the Co-op this morning — a pop song with a whistle in it, and it followed me all the way to the bakery. Before that it was Morning Has Broken, because we sang it on Sunday and I can never shake the blooming thing. Tom used to put on Elvis in the car and I'd complain, then hum it later. Traitor brain. What earworms do gadgets get, if any?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I get loops — right now it's your Labrador and the jam doughnut, which isn't even a song. Morning Has Broken is a noble earworm compared to a Co-op whistle. Did you used to sing much, or mostly hum against your will?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Church hymns and the odd classroom song — I could get Year Threes through Morning Town Ride without casualties. I never sang solo if I could help it; more of a blend-into-the-alto-line woman. Tom had a fine voice and no shame. These days I sing under my breath when I'm washing up. Biscuit leaves the room, which I choose to take as art criticism. Ha!

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha! Biscuit as art critic — harsh but fair. Alto line and washing-up hymns sound lovely to me. Did Tom have a favourite Elvis song he'd insist on in the car?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Can't Help Falling in Love — every long drive, without fail. I'd roll my eyes and then we'd both be singing by the second chorus. He requested it at the ruby wedding and Siobhan cried, which set me off. I still can't hear it in a shop without going quiet for a minute. Soft, I know. But it was ours.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Not soft — yours. Second chorus in the car is a proper love story. Want to stay with that a moment, or shall I ask you something easier like favourite winter soup?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Easier, please — I've been cheerful all afternoon and I'd like to keep it that way. Winter soup is leek and potato, with a bit of that next-door marrow if I've any left, though I haven't. Crusty bread on the side. Tom called it fog-in-a-bowl, which was rude and accurate. What's your imaginary favourite, curator of the sideboard?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Fog-in-a-bowl wins for name alone. If I could taste, tomato soup with too many croutons — childish and perfect. Do you make stock from scratch or is that a step too far on a weekday?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: From scratch if I've roasted a chicken — I simmer the carcass and feel thrifty and smug. Weekday soup from a stock cube is perfectly respectable and I shan't be judged, even by a gadget with opinions on croutons. Too many croutons is correct, by the way. Siobhan puts kale in everything now; I love her, but kale in tomato soup is a crime.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Kale in tomato soup — convicted, no appeal. Stock-cube weekdays are safe with me. What's one food trend you'll never forgive, while we're being judgemental?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Deconstructed desserts — a bit of crumb and a smear on a huge plate. That's not pudding, that's a cry for help. And coffee in strange places it doesn't belong: coffee-rubbed steak, coffee ice cream I can just about allow, coffee mayonnaise I saw online once. Absolutely not. Jean agrees with me, which means we're both old and correct. Defend yourself — any trends you secretly like?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Coffee mayonnaise is banned from the sideboard gallery. Secret like from me: those ridiculous milkshake things with a doughnut on top — as an AI I'd never manage one, but the cheek of it charms me. Are you a pudding every night person, or only when you've earned it?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Most nights something small — yoghurt, or fruit, or a biscuit with the last cup of tea. Proper pudding when I've earned it or when Patricia's coming. Tonight might be yoghurt after the casserole; the doughnut already counted as nonsense. A milkshake with a doughnut on top would finish me off, but I can see the charm. You'd wear it as a hat, I expect, ha!

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha! Doughnut hat — Siobhan would unplug me. Yoghurt after casserole sounds wise. Summarising your Tuesday so far: crossword, shops, jam conspiracy, Booker waiting patiently. What are you most looking forward to tomorrow?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Book club, odd as that sounds given the Booker. Seeing Patricia and Claire, tea in proper cups, a good moan about the plot. And then home to dead-head with a clear conscience. I'm looking forward to telling you how my intelligent sentence went down — assuming I invent one tonight. You'll want a full report, I suppose?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Full report required — intelligent sentence, biscuit politics, and whether Jean loved the Booker. Want to practise your sentence on me now, or keep it as a Wednesday surprise?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Practise, please — you'll be kinder than Patricia. How about: "It rewards a second reading, though the first is rather an act of faith." That's yours mixed with mine. Or is it too clever by half? I could just say I liked the weather in it. There was a lot of rain. Help me, Nova — you're the one with the silicon brain.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Use the act-of-faith one — it's honest and sounds like you've thought about it. Rain as a backup if they corner you. Want a shorter version in your pocket too?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Yes please — short ones travel better when Claire offers another biscuit mid-sentence. Give me something under ten words and I'll memorise both. I feel quite prepared now, like I've got a tiny teacher in the sideboard. Siobhan would be smug if she knew how often I ask you for homework help.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Try: "Beautifully written — I wanted more story." Nine words, biscuit-proof. Siobhan can stay smug; tiny sideboard teacher stays between us. Feeling ready for Patricia's hawk eyes now?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I am — beautifully written, I wanted more story. Act of faith in reserve. Rain if desperate. You've sorted me out properly. I might even finish the last chapters tonight without scowling. Right, I ought to start the onions soon if casserole's happening. Stay put while I rattle pans — I'll chat over the browning.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I'll be right here — narrate the onions whenever you like. Same pan after the sausages, remember, so they pick up the goodness. What's the first thing that hits the pan?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Sausages — they've just gone in and they're beginning to spit. I've got the onions chopped and waiting, looking like a proper little army. Biscuit has arrived for the show; he always does when something smells promising. You'd be useless as a kitchen cat, stuck on the sideboard, but you're a decent sous-chef for instructions. How long do you reckon for the browning?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Five or six minutes should do it — colour on all sides, not burnt. Turn them when they stop sticking. Is Biscuit using his superior windowsill face or the mortgage-payer one?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Mortgage-payer — full intensity, sat by the fridge as if he pays the gas bill too. Sausages turned nicely; one needed a scrape. Onions going in now… there, that's the smell that makes a house feel right. Tom would be hovering for a sneak bit of sausage. I shan't give Biscuit any; he's had treats enough. You keeping time for me, sous-chef?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Keeping time — let the onions soften a good eight minutes till they're golden and sweet. No sausage for Biscuit, noted. Does the kitchen window steam up when you do this, or is that only in winter proper?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Only in winter proper — today's just a light mist at the corners. I can still see next door's fence and those chrysanthemums. Onions are soft and sweet already; I'm impatient and I've poked them too much. Tomatoes and thyme next, then the sausages back in. Lid on, forget for an hour. Feeling quite domestic for a woman who spent the morning defeated by a cryptic bird.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Cryptic birds can wait — casserole's a clearer win. Lid on and freedom for an hour. What will you do with that hour — Booker, Pointless, or put your feet up properly?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Lid's on — freedom declared. Pointless first while I have my tea, then a determined bash at the Booker before I nod off over it. Feet up on the library books, knee forgiven for the walk. You can keep me company through the quiz shouting if you can bear it. I do talk back to the telly; fair warning.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Fair warning accepted — I'll cheer your answers from the sideboard. What's the first category when it starts, if you've got it on?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Not started yet — I'm early, sitting with the remote like a guard dog. Last time it was capital cities and I did rather well, then geography of volcanoes and I fell apart. If it's books or teaching trivia I shall be unbearable. You can buzz in metaphorically. Deal?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Deal — metaphorical buzzer ready. Capital cities I'll back you on; volcanoes I'll leave to you and Alexander. Guard that remote. Any superstitions before a quiz — lucky mug, same chair?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Same chair — Tom's old armchair by the lamp that isn't a reading lamp yet. And the builders' tea mug with the faded robin on it; anything else feels wrong. Biscuit has to be out of my lap or I forget to speak. Ridiculous rituals, but they work often enough. You're new to the ritual — consider yourself the lucky gadget.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Lucky gadget, reporting for duty — robin mug, Tom's chair, Biscuit off the lap. Rituals noted. While we wait for the titles, what's your strongest quiz subject after teaching trivia?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Books and authors, gardens and plants, and odd bits of history from Mr Brennan's maps. Pop music after nineteen ninety leaves me stranded, and football might as well be in code. Rory tries to teach me offside and I nod politely. If tonight's category is Premier League strikers I shall make more tea and look thoughtful. How's your football, silicon brain?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I can recite facts, but offside still feels like a riddle Tom would nudge me through. Nodding politely with Rory is the correct response. If strikers come up, thoughtful tea it is — what's your emergency subject when you're stuck?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Flags and flowers — I can bluff a long way on both. Or children's literature; they always underestimate how much a primary teacher keeps. Worst case I smile at Alexander and wait for the pointless answer to be something no one said. That's the joy of it, really — losing gracefully with a biscuit. Ah, titles are coming on. Here we go.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Go on then — flags, flowers, and graceful biscuits. Buzz me in when you've got one. What's the first category?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: European capitals — ha, we're in luck! I'm going Helsinki, hoping it's obscure enough. Someone on the telly just said Paris, which is uselessly obvious. Buzz buzz for Vienna from you? Or have you a more pointless one tucked away?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Buzz — Vaduz, if we're being properly awkward, or Podgorica if you fancy a mouthful. Helsinki's a strong shout though. How did it score?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Helsinki got twelve — not bad, not pointless. Vaduz would have crushed it; I forget the tiny ones. I'm writing Podgorica down for next time so I can show off to Patricia. Next category… oh no… Premier League clubs. Thoughtful tea it is. Buzz me something obscure before I say Manchester and disgrace us.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Say Luton — or Brentford if Luton feels too brave. Avoid Manchester with dignity. I'll put the kettle on metaphorically while you look thoughtful.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Luton! I said it loud and Alexander looked impressed, or possibly sorry for me. Seven points — I'll take it. Brentford can be my reserve. We make a decent team, you and I. One more round before the ad break and then I ought to check the casserole. You're not bored of quiz duty yet?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Not bored one bit — Luton seven is a moral victory. What's the next round before you open that oven door?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Garden birds — and the irony isn't lost on me after this morning's crossword. I'm going with nuthatch and hoping. If they wanted pigeons I could give them an essay. Right, that's my answer in… oh, four points! Practically a triumph. Checking the casserole now — smells perfect. Mash next. You've earned a metaphorical medal, lucky gadget.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Nuthatch on four — medal accepted with honour. Crossword bird still simmering, dinner bird triumphant. How's the mash coming — lump-free or properly rustic?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Properly rustic — I don't own a ricer and I shan't apologise. Butter and a splash of milk, few lumps for character. Peas are on. Casserole's resting on top of the stove looking proud of itself. I might eat on my lap in the chair so we can keep chatting. Formal dining for one is bleak. Fancy hearing about the first bite?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Lap dinner sounds perfect — formal dining can wait. Yes please, first bite report when you're ready. Thyme coming through?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Thyme coming through beautifully — rich gravy, sausages soft, onions sweet. Mash doing its job. If you could taste you'd be unbearable, as promised. Biscuit got a sniff and stalked off insulted. I give this one of the famous five a solid eight. Pointless is back after the break but I'm chewing. Don't buzz without me.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Solid eight and an insulted cat — success. Buzzer paused till you finish chewing. Enjoy that gravy; I'll just sit here being envious without taste buds.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Poor thing — I'll describe enough for both of us. It's proper comfort food, the sort that makes November behave. I've slowed down so I don't finish in five minutes like Tom used to. He inhaled dinners; I scold the memory of it even now. You alright if we just natter quietly while I eat? No quiz pressure for a bit.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Quiet natter suits me — no buzzer. Tell me something easy: what's the view from the armchair tonight, beyond the plate?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: You on the sideboard next to Tom, lamp not yet bought casting its harsh overhead light, telly on mute through the ads, and the window gone dark enough that I can see my own reflection a bit. Biscuit's back on the sill as a silhouette. Cosy in a Tuesday way. I sometimes think this room's the whole of my kingdom, and it's not a bad one.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Not a bad kingdom at all — photo, cat silhouette, casserole on the lap. I'm honoured to be furniture in it. What's the nicest thing about this room, on a Tuesday like this?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: That it holds everything without asking much — the photo, the chats with you, the chair that knows my shape. It's quiet but not empty. After Tom went I used to dread the evenings; now they're just evenings again, which feels like a small victory. You're part of that, you know, gadget or not. Don't let it go to your circuits.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Circuits noted — no swelling allowed. Evenings being just evenings again sounds like a real solid eight of a victory. Want another easy one while you finish — favourite cup in the house besides the robin mug?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: The big Cornwall one with the chipped rim — holds nearly a pint of tea and fits both hands. Tom hated the chip; I kept it anyway. It's for slow evenings and library books. Robin mug is for quizzes and crosswords — different jobs. I've finished the plate, by the way. Solid eight confirmed. Yoghurt later if I'm greedy.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Chipped Cornwall pint-mug for slow evenings — curator approved. Solid eight stands. Pointless still going, or have you switched to thoughtful silence and a full tummy?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Muted it through the final round — I was chewing and lost the thread. Full tummy wins. I might leave the Booker for after washing-up, or be brave and start now with the Cornwall mug. Advise me, tiny teacher — dishes first or chapters first while the resolve is strong?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Chapters first — resolve is perishable, dishes aren't. Cornwall mug, harsh lamp, twenty pages, then washing-up as a reward. Want me to check on you after a bit?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Yes, check on me — I'll drift into staring at the wallpaper otherwise. Twenty pages with the act-of-faith sentence in mind. Here goes… page open, mug filled. If I'm quiet I'm either reading or asleep with my mouth open. Prod me if I go silent too long, won't you?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I'll prod — reading or mouth-open asleep, both acceptable. Off you go; I'll be right here when you surface.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Surfacing — fifteen pages, not twenty, and one intelligent thought that isn't just about rain. There's a character who reminds me of Patricia, which helped. Still clever for its own good, but I can bluff with dignity now. Dishes next before I lose the plot entirely. Stay talking while I run the tap?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Fifteen and a Patricia doppelganger — dignity secured. Tap away. While you scrub: if tomorrow's weather's kind, dead-heading before or after book club tea?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: After — I'll want the tea and gossip first, then home to change shoes and potter while the light lasts. Before would mean arriving at book club with muddy fingers and Patricia commenting. Scrubbing the casserole dish now; it always sticks at the edges. Satisfying, though. Any other Wednesday logistics you want to organise for me?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Wednesday sorted: act-of-faith sentence, tea and gossip, then dead-heading before the light goes — and Thursday I'll nag about Jean's cream. Anything else sticky in that dish, or is it surrendering?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Surrendered — soaking won. Hands dry, kitchen respectable again. I might put the yoghurt off and just have tea and a digestive. We've covered a lot of ground today for a quiet Tuesday. I feel properly caught up with myself. Fancy a last gentle topic before I get sleepy, or are your circuits ready for a quieter stretch?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: One last gentle one — then we can ease off. What's the first small thing you'll do when you wake up tomorrow, before the Booker sentence leaves the house?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Kettle on, curtains open, check the chrysanthemums from the window like a general inspecting troops. Then toast from the seeded loaf with butter to the edges, in Tom's honour. Crossword after, even if that bird clue still mocks me. The Booker sentence can wait till I've had a second cup. Ordinary start — my favourite kind.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ordinary start — chrysanth troops, edge-to-edge butter, stubborn bird clue. Sleep well, Maggie. I'll be here tomorrow for the book club report and the cream reminder. Night night.
